examTakeaway: Crossed pain and temperature loss, Horner syndrome, and dysphagia are a lateral medullary infarct.
scenario: A 66-year-old man suddenly has vertigo and hiccups. The left side of his face and the right side of his body do not feel pinprick. The left pupil is small and the left eyelid is droopy. He coughs when he swallows. Strength in the arms and legs is preserved.
question: Which vessel is occluded?
options: Left anterior inferior cerebellar artery only, sparing the lateral medulla
explanation: Crossed pain and temperature loss, Horner syndrome, and dysphagia are a lateral medullary infarct. Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies that lateral medulla, where the spinal trigeminal nucleus, spinothalamic tract, and sympathetic fibers sit. Anterior spinal artery infarction is a medial cord or medial medullary syndrome with weakness, not this crossed sensory pattern. Left anterior cerebral artery would weaken the right leg. Right middle cerebral artery would weaken the left face and arm. Left anterior inferior cerebellar artery only, sparing the lateral medulla, can cause facial paralysis and deafness, not this classic lateral medullary pattern.

examTakeaway: Ipsilateral loss of proprioception and contralateral loss of pain, with ipsilateral weakness, is hemisection of the cord.
scenario: A 28-year-old man was stabbed on the left side of the neck. Below the wound, the left arm and leg are weak, vibration is lost on the left, and pinprick is lost on the right. The right side is strong.
question: Which cord pattern is this?
explanation: Ipsilateral loss of proprioception and contralateral loss of pain, with ipsilateral weakness, is hemisection of the cord. Left hemisection cuts the left corticospinal tract and left dorsal columns before they have clinical effect on the same side, while pain has already crossed, so pinprick is lost on the right. Complete transection would weaken and numb both sides. Central cord syndrome hurts the crossing spinothalamic fibers and weakens the arms more than the legs, usually after hyperextension. Anterior spinal artery infarction spares the dorsal columns. Right hemisection would weaken the right limbs and lose pinprick on the left.

examTakeaway: Shoulder pain, a small pupil, and wasting of the hand intrinsic muscles are an apical lung tumor invading the sympathetic chain.
scenario: A 62-year-old man who smoked for 40 years has pain at the tip of the left shoulder. The left pupil is small, the left eyelid droops, and the left hand intrinsics are wasted. A chest film shows a mass at the left apex.
question: Which structure has the mass invaded?
options: Facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
explanation: Shoulder pain, a small pupil, and wasting of the hand intrinsic muscles are an apical lung tumor invading the sympathetic chain. Cervical sympathetic chain interruption causes Horner syndrome on the same side, and the lower brachial plexus explains the wasted hand. Left recurrent laryngeal nerve only would hoarsen the voice and would not change the pupil. Right sympathetic chain would make the right pupil small. Optic chiasm compression causes a bitemporal field cut, not a small pupil and a wasted hand. Facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen paralyzes the face and spares the pupil.

examTakeaway: Resting tremor, rigidity, and a shuffling gait are loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
scenario: A 68-year-old man has a slow resting tremor of the right hand, a soft voice, and a short-stepped gait. Tone in the arms is increased. A trial of levodopa improves the tremor. There is no weakness.
question: Which neurons have been lost?
options: Cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis
Lower motor neurons of the anterior horn
Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta
correctAnswer: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta
explanation: Resting tremor, rigidity, and a shuffling gait are loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta project to the striatum, and their loss is Parkinson disease, which responds to levodopa. Cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis are lost in Alzheimer disease. GABAergic neurons of the striatum are lost in Huntington disease. Serotonergic neurons of the raphe modulate mood and pain, not this motor picture. Lower motor neurons of the anterior horn are lost in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spinal muscular atrophy, with weakness and fasciculations.

examTakeaway: Chorea, psychiatric change, and a family history are loss of striatal neurons from a CAG expansion in huntingtin.
scenario: A 40-year-old man has had fidgeting movements for a year and has become irritable. His father died in a psychiatric hospital with similar movements. MRI shows atrophy of the caudate. There is no resting tremor.
question: Which cells are lost?
explanation: Chorea, psychiatric change, and a family history are loss of striatal neurons from a CAG expansion in huntingtin. Striatal neurons of the caudate and putamen are the cells that atrophy in Huntington disease. Substantia nigra pars compacta neurons are lost in Parkinson disease, which has a resting tremor he does not have. Cerebellar Purkinje cells only are the target in some spinocerebellar ataxias, not this caudate picture. Anterior horn cells are lost in motor neuron disease. Hippocampal pyramidal cells only are an early site of Alzheimer disease.
